summary: Chris Koerner explains how to start and run a farmer's market (using his wife's kids' market at a shopping centre as the example), then interviews Mike McCoy of Prep Pizza, who sold DIY pizza dough kits at farmer's markets (about $60k in a first summer, part time) before scaling online via Facebook ads to claimed $3-4M of sales. The video also covers other farmer's market products (baked goods, pickles, fresh pasta) and tips such as sampling, choosing in-city markets, and filming content. Key takeaway: farmer's markets are a cheap, fast way to validate a physical food product, and a market organiser can piggyback on a venue that wants footfall.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; launching a powdered drink mix business.

speakers.name: Mike McCoy
speakers.description: Co-founder of Prep Pizza (prepapizza.com), sells pizza dough making kits.

ideas.name: Pizza dough kit (Prep Pizza)
ideas.one_liner: DIY pizza dough ingredient kit with free training course, sold first at farmer's markets then online via Facebook ads.
ideas.business_model: One-off product sales of a $30 kit; free masterclass and support drive conversion and satisfaction.
ideas.customer: Home cooks who want better pizza at home, including the outdoor cooking crowd and people who bought equipment and failed.
ideas.problem: Home cooks struggle to get good pizza dough and revert to store-bought; they lack the right flour, ingredients and technique.
ideas.offer: A kit with flour, yeast, salt, honey powder and diastatic malt powder for roughly six pizzas (2 lb package), a two-part poolish recipe, a free video masterclass, chat and phone support.

pricing.notes: Not the cheapest product; customers often say it is expensive, justified by training and support.

acquisition_channels.details: Farmer's markets 3-4 per week (Wed, Thu, two Saturdays) with a pizza oven, samples of plain dough with minimal toppings; also food shows, golf tournaments and neighbourhood events.

quote.text: I started going farmer's market after farmer's market and basically over the course of a summer, you know, I sold roughly $60,000
quote.speaker: Mike McCoy

acquisition_channels.details: Facebook/Instagram ads; hired an agency first with poor results, then took it over himself; about 60 active ads with frequent creative rotation. Also Google ads.

quote.text: we did in less than 30 days what we did in four months in sales just by me taking out over everything
quote.speaker: Mike McCoy

ideas.delivery: Kits assembled in the founders' basement (weighing ingredients, bagging, sealing machine, batches of ~100), later online order fulfilment; training delivered via a free online course; founder answers chat and phone support himself.
unit_economics_claims: About $60k sold in first summer at markets, under 20 hrs/week
Gross margin about 80% on ingredients (agreed to host's estimate)
Roughly $3-4M online sales over a couple of years
Best farmer's market day close to $3k
ideas.startup_cost: Low; basement production, pre-ordered bags, bulk ingredients, no ad spend at first (amount not stated)
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Immediate at the first farmer's markets; online was dismal for the first four months.

acquisition.how: Facebook/Google ads and creative testing can be largely agent-run; the market phase was in-person and would be 0-1.

onboarding.how: Order confirmation and course access are automated by e-commerce tooling.

delivery.how: Physical kit assembly and shipping; needs a 3PL to reduce human work, otherwise manual packing.

support.how: Chat and email can be handled by an AI agent with the course content; founder currently answers personally.

uk_applicability.notes: Concept works in the UK (farmer's markets, Facebook ads), but food business registration with the local council, allergen labelling, labelling rules and UK flour/yeast sourcing apply; imperial/US cottage food laws differ.

risks: Facebook ad costs consume most margin
Heavy reliance on one ad platform

quotes.text: we charged $30 for our kit, $29.97 online
quotes.speaker: Mike McCoy

quotes.text: every single time I'd walk home without and people would buy them
quotes.speaker: Mike McCoy

ideas.name: Run a farmer's market at a shopping centre
ideas.one_liner: Organise a market on a mixed-use shopping centre's parking spaces and sidewalks, charging vendors booth fees while the venue provides space and promotion.
ideas.customer: Market vendors (and, indirectly, the shopping centre wanting footfall).
ideas.problem: Shopping centres want to look busy and drive traffic; vendors need venues with existing crowds.
ideas.offer: A ready-made market day on venue land with the venue advertising it, vendors bringing their own tents, tables and chairs.

pricing.notes: Host suggests adult markets could charge more.

acquisition_channels.details: Called the shopping centre marketing manager; venue offered roped-off parking, electronic billboard, email list and gift cards for judges.

quote.text: it's in their best interest to host a farmer's market
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

acquisition_channels.details: Piggybacks on the shopping centre's existing audience; vendors' families promote on social media. Small Facebook page (300 followers).

ideas.delivery: Mark booth spots with numbered laminated sheets weighed down with sandbags; vendors set up from 8am, market 9am to 12-2pm; organiser runs the day (judging app built by Chris).
unit_economics_claims: Second market sold 100 booths in about a week
ideas.startup_cost: Almost nothing; the only cost was providing tables and chairs, which they won't repeat.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; first market sold 50 booths over a couple of months.

acquisition.how: Venue outreach and vendor recruitment can be assisted by tooling but the venue deal needs human negotiation.

onboarding.how: Vendor sign-up forms, booth maps and instructions can be automated.

delivery.how: Physical event on a Saturday requires people on-site.

support.how: Vendor questions handled by agent before the event; on-site by humans.

uk_applicability.notes: Works with changes: UK public liability insurance, venue permissions, council street trading rules and food hygiene checks for food vendors.

risks: Revenue claim is hypothetical, based on a non-profit kids' market

tactics.name: Validate food products at farmer's markets
steps: Go to 3-4 markets per week (Wed, Thu, two Saturdays) with 30-40 units
Have the spouse cover a second market on Saturdays
Give samples of the product exactly as sold, with minimal toppings so the product is tasted
Take payment via QR code/Venmo, no team needed
Prefer markets inside city limits that are well marketed

quote.text: every single time I'd walk home without and people would buy them
quote.speaker: Mike McCoy

tactics.name: Move from markets to Facebook ads
steps: Start online once markets prove the product
Test an agency, but be ready to take over marketing yourself
Run many ad creatives (about 60 active) and rotate them often
Use high gross margin to afford ad costs

quote.text: you have to have a way more creatives than you think and you have to rotate them much more often than you think
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Free course and support to increase conversions
steps: Include a free masterclass with every kit
Collect troubleshooting issues and reshoot the course
Offer live chat and an 800 number answered by the founder

tactics.name: Pitch a venue that wants footfall
steps: Contact the shopping centre marketing manager
Offer a market on parking spaces
Ask the venue to advertise on billboard and email list and supply gift cards
Mark booths with laminated numbers weighed with sandbags; vendors bring own tables and chairs

tactics.name: Film content at the market
steps: Set up cameras behind you and let people taste
Do not be abrasive about filming; people ignore it

warnings.warning: Don't provide tables and chairs when running a market; only provide ground space.

quote.text: We provided tables and chairs. Never again, ever, ever again.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

warnings.warning: Cheap knickknacks and crafts sell poorly at kids' markets; higher-ticket $20-50 items do better.
Wanting to open a restaurant because friends love your cooking is a trap; running the business is most of the work.

quote.text: being a good cook is like 20% of it. You still have to run a dang business
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

warnings.warning: Selling prepared food at markets requires permits; samples are generally exempt but laws vary by state.
Not every farmer's market is good; roadside ones outside city limits can have no customers.
Facebook ad spend takes most of the margin and an agency did not work at first.

quote.text: our good friend Zuckerberg gets the majority of our money
quote.speaker: Mike McCoy

lessons.lesson: Farmer's markets are a cheap, fast, real-time feedback channel for physical products before investing in ads.

quote.text: These markets are just an amazing place to get immediate real time feedback from strangers on your product.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

lessons.lesson: High gross margin (about 80%) allows aggressive paid advertising, unlike 10-20% margin competitors.
Piggyback on existing audiences (a shopping centre's traffic) instead of building your own.
Selling a product plus training/support increases success and justifies a premium price.
Taking over marketing yourself and learning it produced more in 30 days than four months with an agency.
Choose businesses you are passionate about when you can afford to.
Selling a product around a hobby is lower-risk than opening a restaurant.
Some customers only buy at the market and distrust the internet; online conversion is a separate problem.

evidence_quality.rationale: First-hand operator with specific headline numbers (60k summer, 160k best month, 3-4M online) but unverified, little detail on ad spend or profit. The farmer's market organiser economics are hypothetical. Whisper-tiny transcript contains mishearings.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Chris promotes TKOwners.com community and his own Busy Juice; Mike promotes prepapizza.com.
